protocol: Deterministic multi-turn driver-feedback demo using the real saved M1.2 XGBoost models, instance-level SHAP explanations, the synthetic RAG corpus, and the M4.4 DriverConversationService. No models are retrained; no preprocessors refitted; no source artifacts are modified.

evidence_backed.statement: The retrieved material noted the following (synthetic educational content, not a verified measurement).
evidence_backed.excerpt: Do not feed consumed-fuel increments or cumulative trip fuel into a model that predicts instantaneous fuel rate: these are integrals of the target and leak the answer. Exclude them, and never give the model future timestamps or future telemetry.

evidence_backed.statement: The retrieved material noted the following (synthetic educational content, not a verified measurement).
evidence_backed.excerpt: Frequent acceleration and braking wastes fuel because energy put into accelerating is then dissipated as heat in braking. Smooth driving with steady speed, gentle throttle and anticipation of stops lowers average fuel use relative to aggressive stop-and-go driving.

evidence_backed.statement: The retrieved material noted the following (synthetic educational content, not a verified measurement).
evidence_backed.excerpt: Fuel consumption of a heavy-duty truck is primarily driven by the power demanded at the wheels, which depends on the vehicle mass, speed, acceleration, aerodynamic drag, rolling resistance and road gradient. Higher demanded power requires more fuel per second. The fuel rate (L/h) is therefore an immediate proxy for engine load and driver demand, not a fixed vehicle property.

evidence_backed.statement: The retrieved material noted the following (synthetic educational content, not a verified measurement).
evidence_backed.excerpt: In the datasets in this project, fuel rate is reported in litres per hour (L/h). Values range from near idle (a few L/h) up to well over 100 L/h during hard acceleration or climbing under load. Always convert to consistent units before comparing.

evidence_backed.excerpt: Driver feedback on fuel use should be constructive, specific and non-judgemental. It must never encourage unsafe behaviour such as aggressive coasting downhill, exceeding speed limits, or shutting off the engine in traffic. Safety always outranks fuel economy.

verification.synthetic_corruption_or_environment_note: The demo runs on a synthetic telemetry-derived model and a synthetic knowledge corpus; outputs are model estimates, not real-world observations.

limitations: Synthetic data: predictions, explanations, and retrieved passages are all derived from synthetic telemetry / a synthetic corpus. They are not validated real-world fuel measurements or manufacturer guidance.
SHAP contributions describe how the model composes its prediction; they are not causal evidence about real-world fuel consumption.
The demo exercises the deterministic, rule-based routing path; it is not an LLM and does not generate free-form natural language.
Only the scenario inputs exercised here are shown; the demo is a representative workflow, not an exhaustive coverage of all driver phrasings.
Retrieval similarity is not proof of factual correctness; evidence sufficiency is judged against a documented heuristic similarity floor.
